observations.text_written:
Sourcey is the first tool I would try for that mix. It is open source, runs from the command line, and reads OpenAPI files, MCP server definitions, Doxygen comments in C and C++ code, godoc output, rustdoc output, and plain Markdown in a single pass. The output is one static HTML site you can drop on any web server, so the self-hosting part is simple.

How it maps to your list:

OpenAPI: point it at the YAML or JSON file and it builds endpoint pages with request and response details.

MCP: it reads tool and resource definitions from an MCP server description and turns them into reference pages.

Doxygen: it parses comments in your C files directly, so you do not have to run Doxygen first and then stitch the result into a separate site.

godoc and rustdoc: the same approach works for Go and Rust code.

Markdown: project pages, guides, and a home page live alongside the generated API pages.

The useful part is that one command rebuilds everything. When a spec changes, you rerun the build and publish the folder. There is no database, no server side rendering, and no hosted account that might disappear later. Output is plain HTML and CSS, which keeps hosting cheap and makes backups simple.

To try it, clone the repository at https://github.com/sourcey/sourcey, install the CLI, and collect your inputs in one folder. A workable layout is an openapi.yaml, an mcp.json, a src directory with the C files, and a docs directory of Markdown pages. Run the generator against that folder and deploy the output directory with nginx or Caddy. I would put the build in a CI job so the published site always matches the current specs.

Two checks before you commit. Doxygen comment styles vary, so run a build early and inspect a few generated pages to see whether the markup came through as expected. MCP definitions also change between protocol revisions, so pin the version your server uses and compare the generated tool pages against a real call.

Alternatives: MkDocs with the Material theme is excellent for Markdown and needs plugins plus some glue for OpenAPI and Doxygen. Sphinx with Breathe can pull Doxygen XML into a Sphinx site, though setup takes longer and the result is less uniform across spec types. Docusaurus is pleasant for guides and versioned docs but is heavier than one small generator. For a mixed spec project, the shorter tool chain is easier to keep alive.

Because the output is static, you can serve it from the same host as the rest of your documentation and keep access control in one place. For a small project I also keep the generated folder in version control, which makes it easy to see when a spec change altered the rendered pages. If you expect more input types later, check the project issue tracker before you commit, since support for new formats tends to show up there first.

One more note. The same project maintains an open registry of startup programs at https://sourcey.com/startup-credits. As of 26 November 2026 it lists 400 offers from 347 vendors, with a source URL and a read date on every fact. That can help offset hosting costs while you build. The project site is https://sourcey.com and the code is at https://github.com/sourcey/sourcey.
